questions.stem: A patient takes isophane insulin at 7 AM plus rapid-acting insulin with breakfast. Low blood sugar happens around 3 PM. Which insulin is the likely cause?

options.text: Neither insulin; insulin cannot cause this

questions.explanation: B is correct: 3 PM is 8 hours after the 7 AM dose, inside isophane's 4 to 12 hour peak. A is wrong because rapid-acting insulin lasts about 3 to 5 hours and was gone by late morning. C is wrong because insulin causes low sugar. D ignores the timing: only isophane is still peaking.

questions.stem: When should lispro be given for a meal?
questions.explanation: D is correct: rapid-acting insulins like lispro start in about 15 minutes, so give them right before the meal. A is too early; sugar can drop before food arrives. C is the wrong time for a mealtime insulin. B is too late to cover the meal.

questions.stem: When should regular insulin be given for a meal?
questions.explanation: A is correct: regular insulin starts in about 30 minutes, so give it about 30 minutes before eating. B is too late to cover the meal. C is far too early; regular lasts only up to about 8 hours. D does not cover the meal.

questions.stem: Which statements about isophane insulin are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Roll the vial or pen gently; do not shake it
It peaks about 4 to 12 hours after the dose
It can last up to about 24 hours

questions.explanation: B, C, D, and E are correct: isophane is cloudy, is rolled gently, peaks around 4 to 12 hours, and can last up to about 24 hours. A is wrong: the flat, no-peak pattern describes long-acting basal insulins like glargine.

questions.stem: Regular insulin and isophane insulin are being mixed in one syringe. Which is drawn up first?
questions.explanation: B is correct: draw up clear before cloudy, so regular goes first. A reverses the order and can put cloudy insulin into the clear vial. C ignores the rule. D is wrong because regular and isophane can be mixed; it is glargine that must never be mixed.

questions.stem: A patient asks to mix glargine with lispro in one syringe to cut down on injections. What is the best response?

options.text: Never mix glargine with any other insulin
Mix them only in a pen

questions.explanation: C is correct: never mix glargine in the same syringe with any other insulin. A applies the regular-and-isophane mixing rule to glargine, which must not be mixed. B and D still mix glargine.

questions.stem: A prescriber orders 100 units of concentrated regular insulin, 500 units per mL, using its dedicated syringe. What volume is that?
questions.explanation: C is correct: 100 units divided by 500 units per mL is 0.2 mL. A is the volume for standard 100 units per mL insulin, which would be five times too much here. B and D do not match 100 divided by 500.

questions.stem: An order reads: insulin regular 10 U subcutaneously. What is the best pharmacist action?

options.text: Clarify the order so units is written in full

questions.explanation: D is correct: a letter U can be misread as a zero, turning 10 units into 100, so clarify and have units written in full. A dispenses an error-prone order. C makes the exact misreading the rule is meant to prevent. B changes the drug without a reason.

questions.stem: Which insulin storage teaching is correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep unopened insulin in the refrigerator
Most opened pens and vials are good at room temperature for about 28 days; check each label

questions.explanation: B, C, and D are correct: unopened insulin goes in the refrigerator, never the freezer, and most opened pens and vials last about 28 days at room temperature, checking each label. A is wrong because insulin must never be frozen. E is wrong because most opened products last about 28 days, not 90.

questions.stem: A patient on insulin has low blood sugar and cannot swallow safely. What is the best treatment?
questions.explanation: A is correct: if the patient cannot swallow safely, give glucagon. B gives sugar by mouth to someone who cannot swallow safely. C lowers sugar further. D delays treatment while sugar stays low.
